title: Say hello
subtitle: Greetings & basic manners
intro: Emiratis greet warmly and often. mar7aba and ahlan both mean "hello" — mix in shukran (thanks) and ma3a el salaamah (goodbye) and you can open and close almost any conversation. 3 and 7 stand in for Arabic sounds English doesn't have (ain and ha) — you'll see them everywhere.

title: Talking about yourself
subtitle: Pronouns — I, you, he, she...
intro: Pronouns are the words you swap in for names: ana (I), enta/enty (you, m/f), huwa/hiya (he/she). You'll lean on these constantly once you start building sentences — today's the day to lock them in.

title: Counting in Arabic
subtitle: Numbers 0–100
intro: Numbers 0–10 are your building blocks — the teens just tack "3ash" on the end, and the tens (3ashreen, thalatheen...) all rhyme. Learn these once and prices, ages, and phone numbers stop being a guessing game.

title: Meet the family
subtitle: Family vocabulary
intro: Family comes up constantly in Emirati small talk — people ask about your family before they ask about your job. Umm (mother), abo (father), ukho (brother), ekht (sister) are the core four; we'll build out uncles, aunts, and grandparents too.

title: Asking questions
subtitle: Question words — shu, wain, kam...
intro: shu (what), wain (where), kam (how much/many), laish (why) — these question words are how you turn a vocabulary list into a real conversation. Combine them with what you already know: "wain el bait?" (where is the house?).

title: Present-tense verbs
subtitle: Grammar: conjugating verbs happening now
intro: Present-tense verbs change shape depending on who's doing the action — add a- for "I", te- for "you", ye- for "he", and so on. Once you know the pattern, you can conjugate almost any verb in this app, not just the handful of examples.

title: Everyday food & drink
subtitle: Food vocabulary
intro: gahwa (coffee), chai (tea), and khebz (bread) will get you through most menus. Emirati meals lean on rice (3aish), meat (la7am), and generous portions — order with abgha or atlab ("I want / I'll order").

title: Ownership — mine, yours, ours
subtitle: Grammar: possessive suffixes
intro: Instead of a separate word for "my", Emirati Arabic just adds an ending to the noun: sayyaarah (car) → sayyaarty (my car). Same idea as verbs — one small suffix per person, attached straight to the word.

title: Finding your way
subtitle: Directions & places
intro: yemeen (right), yesaar (left), sayda (straight) — combine these with places like elmataar (the airport) or elmadrasah (the school) and you can direct a taxi anywhere. jeddaam (in front of) and wara (behind) round out the picture.

title: Prepositions in context
subtitle: Grammar: fi, 3ala, ma3, min, ila, bayn
intro: Prepositions glue sentences together — fi (in), 3ala (on), ma3 (with), min (from), ila (to), bayn (between). Today's practice drops them into real sentences instead of flashcards, so you learn them the way you'll actually use them.

title: Talking about the past
subtitle: Grammar: past-tense verbs
intro: Past tense drops the prefix from class 6 and adds a suffix instead: root + -t for "I", root alone for "he", root + -aw for "they". We'll reuse the same verbs you conjugated in present tense — daras (studied), la3ab (played) — just with new endings.

title: Culture & everyday life
subtitle: Capstone — culture vocab + a real conversation
intro: The majlis (sitting room) and dallah (coffee pot) sit at the center of Emirati hospitality and karam (generosity). For your final class, you'll finish with a full conversation between two friends catching up — pulling together family words, verbs, and places from everything you've learned so far.
